blocks.text: Every vector space, whether it is the familiar 2D plane or a 300 dimensional embedding space, can be described completely using a small handful of reference vectors instead of infinitely many points. This lesson covers exactly what makes a set of vectors qualify as that reference set, called a basis, and how counting the vectors in it gives the single number known as dimension.

blocks.alt: Overview of basis and dimension concepts
blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What a Basis Is

A basis for a vector space is a set of vectors that satisfies two conditions at once: the vectors must span the whole space, meaning every point in that space can be reached by combining them, and the vectors must be linearly independent, meaning none of them is redundant, expressible as a combination of the others.

blocks.alt: The two standard basis vectors of the 2D plane
blocks.caption: e1 and e2 together span the entire plane and are independent

blocks.text: Both requirements matter equally: a set that spans but is not independent has redundant vectors it does not need, and a set that is independent but does not span cannot reach every point in the space.

A basis is not unique to a space, many different valid bases can describe the exact same space, the way section 5.1 demonstrates, but every space still has at least one, and typically infinitely many, valid choices.
2. Span: What a Set of Vectors Can Reach

The span of a set of vectors is every point reachable by scaling and adding them together in any combination. Two independent 2D vectors already span the entire plane, since scaling and adding them can produce any point at all.

code.content:
import numpy as np
e1 = np.array([1, 0])
e2 = np.array([0, 1])
target = np.array([7, -3])
# target = 7*e1 + (-3)*e2, so target is in the span of e1 and e2

blocks.text: A single vector by itself only spans a line through the origin, never a full 2D plane, no matter how it is scaled. Reaching a full plane requires at least two independent directions.

Span answers only the reachability half of the basis question, it says nothing about redundancy, which is exactly why independence, covered next in section 3, is still needed to complete the definition of a basis.
3. Linear Independence Recap

Linear independence was first covered properly in the rank of matrix lesson: a set of vectors is independent when none of them can be written as a combination of the others. A basis requires this because a redundant vector adds no new reachable point, it only adds an unnecessary extra vector to carry around.

code.content:
v1 = np.array([1, 2])
v2 = np.array([2, 4])   # exactly 2 times v1, redundant
A = np.array([v1, v2])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))   # 1, confirming redundancy, not 2 independent directions

blocks.text: This is the same rank test used throughout the rank of matrix lesson, applied here specifically to check whether a candidate set of basis vectors is safe to use, rather than to diagnose a general matrix.
4. The Standard Basis

The most familiar basis for ordinary coordinate space is the standard basis: (1, 0) and (0, 1) in 2D, or (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1) in 3D, and so on. Every coordinate you have ever written down, like the point (3, 5), is secretly already expressed as coefficients against this standard basis: 3 times (1, 0) plus 5 times (0, 1).

code.content:
e1, e2, e3 = np.eye(3)   # the 3 rows of the identity matrix are the standard basis of 3D space
point = np.array([2, -1, 4])
# point = 2*e1 + (-1)*e2 + 4*e3

blocks.text: This is exactly why the identity matrix lesson called the identity matrix a do-nothing matrix, its columns are precisely the standard basis, so multiplying by it reconstructs any vector using its own standard coordinates unchanged.

The standard basis is popular specifically because it is already orthonormal, each vector has unit length and is perpendicular to every other, which is exactly the convenient property the orthogonality lesson highlighted as ideal for a basis to have.
5. Dimension: Counting the Basis Vectors

The dimension of a vector space is simply the number of vectors needed in any basis for that space. The ordinary plane is 2 dimensional because its basis needs exactly 2 vectors, ordinary 3D space is 3 dimensional because its basis needs exactly 3.
5.1 Why Every Basis Has the Same Size

A given space can have many different valid bases, but every single one of them, no matter how they are chosen, always contains exactly the same number of vectors. This is why dimension is a well defined, fixed property of the space itself, not an accident of which particular basis happened to be picked.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: The 2D plane has infinitely many valid bases, (1, 0) and (0, 1), or (1, 1) and (1, negative 1), or (2, 0) and (0, 3), but every single one of them contains exactly 2 vectors. Trying to span the 2D plane with only 1 vector always fails, and any 3 vectors in the 2D plane are automatically dependent, since the space only has room for 2 independent directions.

blocks.text: 6. Change of Basis

The same point can be described using different coordinates depending on which basis is being used, since coordinates are always coefficients relative to some chosen basis, not an absolute property of the point itself. Converting a point coordinates from one basis to another is called a change of basis.

code.content:
B = np.array([[1, 1], [1, -1]]).T   # a new basis: columns (1,1) and (1,-1)
point_standard = np.array([4, 2])    # coordinates in the standard basis
point_in_B = np.linalg.inv(B).dot(point_standard)   # coordinates in the new basis B
print(point_in_B)   # [3. 1.]

blocks.text: Multiplying those new coordinates back by B reconstructs the original point exactly, confirming that a change of basis never actually moves the point, it only changes the numbers used to describe where it sits.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Describing a location as 3 blocks north and 2 blocks east assumes a north-east basis. Describing that exact same location relative to a diagonal street grid instead gives entirely different numbers, yet the physical location on the ground never changes, only the basis used to describe it does.

blocks.text: 7. Verifying a Basis in Code

Checking whether a proposed set of vectors is actually a valid basis for a space of a known dimension comes down to two checks: counting whether there are exactly the right number of vectors, and confirming they are independent using the rank test from the rank of matrix lesson.

code.content:
candidate = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 1]])
is_right_count = candidate.shape[0] == 2       # 2 vectors, matches 2D space
is_independent = np.linalg.matrix_rank(candidate) == 2
print(is_right_count and is_independent)   # True, valid basis for 2D space

blocks.text: Both checks are needed together, a set can pass the count check while still failing the independence check, exactly the redundant-vector scenario covered back in section 3.
8. Basis and Rank: The Same Idea, Two Names

The rank of a matrix, covered in the rank of matrix lesson, is exactly the dimension of the space spanned by its rows, or equivalently its columns. Put differently, the rank of a matrix is the size of a basis for its own row space or column space, rank and dimension are the same underlying concept viewed from two different angles.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [0, 1, 1]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))   # 2, meaning the row space of A is 2 dimensional, a basis for it needs only 2 vectors

blocks.text: This reframing means every intuition already built for rank, invertibility depending on full rank, a zero eigenvalue signaling rank deficiency, transfers directly onto dimension and basis without needing to relearn anything new.
9. Overcomplete and Underdetermined Sets

A set with more vectors than the dimension of the space is called overcomplete, it necessarily contains at least one redundant, dependent vector and therefore cannot be a basis on its own. A set with fewer vectors than the dimension is underdetermined, it cannot possibly span the whole space no matter how it is combined.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Set size vs dimension","Can it be a basis?","Why"],"rows":[["fewer vectors than dimension","no","cannot span the full space, some directions are unreachable"],["exactly equal to dimension, independent","yes","exactly enough vectors, none redundant"],["more vectors than dimension","no","guaranteed to contain at least one dependent, redundant vector"]]}

blocks.text: This table is a useful sanity check any time a proposed basis is being assembled by hand: count the vectors first, then confirm independence, since either check failing on its own is enough to rule the set out as a basis.
10. Dimension in AI: Embedding Spaces

Every embedding vector produced by a language model, image model, or recommendation system lives in a space with a fixed, chosen dimension, commonly numbers like 384, 768, or 1536. That number is literally the dimension covered in this lesson: the number of independent directions the model has available to represent meaning in.

items: A higher embedding dimension gives more independent directions to separate distinct concepts, at the cost of more memory and compute per vector.
Reducing an embedding down to a smaller dimension, using PCA in the lesson ahead, is exactly finding a smaller basis that still captures most of the useful structure.
Feature engineering in classical machine learning is, in this same language, a decision about which basis, which set of measured quantities, best describes the underlying data.

blocks.text: Choosing an embedding dimension is itself a basis-size decision made by whoever designs the model, too small a dimension behaves like an underdetermined set from section 9, unable to represent every distinction that matters, while an unnecessarily large dimension wastes memory on directions that carry little real information.
11. Orthogonal Bases Are the Best Kind

The orthogonality lesson showed that when a basis is also orthogonal, or better yet orthonormal, extracting coordinates against it becomes a single dot product instead of a full change-of-basis computation like the one in section 6. Whenever there is a choice, an orthonormal basis is almost always preferred for exactly this reason.

code.content:
B_orthonormal = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]])   # already orthonormal
point = np.array([4, 2])
coef1 = np.dot(point, B_orthonormal[0])   # 4, no inverse needed
coef2 = np.dot(point, B_orthonormal[1])   # 2, no inverse needed

blocks.text: Gram-Schmidt, covered in the orthogonality lesson, exists specifically to convert any valid but non-orthogonal basis into this preferred, orthonormal form, without changing the space it spans.
12. Subspaces and Basis of a Subspace

A subspace is a smaller vector space living entirely inside a larger one, such as a single 2 dimensional plane sitting inside 3 dimensional space, and it always requires its own smaller basis. The column space and row space introduced in the rank of matrix lesson are exactly such subspaces, and their dimension is exactly the rank of the matrix that produced them.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2, 0], [2, 4, 0], [0, 0, 1]])
# column space is spanned by only 2 independent columns, a 2D subspace inside 3D space
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A))   # 2, the dimension of that subspace

blocks.text: Every subspace, no matter how it arises, always has a well defined dimension of its own, which can never exceed the dimension of the larger space it lives inside.
13. Basis and Dimensionality Reduction

Reducing the dimension of a dataset always means the same underlying operation: replacing the original basis with a smaller one that still captures most of what matters. Every dimensionality reduction technique, from simply dropping a redundant feature to running full PCA, is a variation on choosing a smaller, better basis.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A dataset with both temperature in Celsius and temperature in Fahrenheit as separate columns is secretly 1 dimensional in that regard, since the second column is always a fixed linear function of the first. Dropping one of them is the simplest possible form of dimensionality reduction: recognizing that the current basis, the two temperature columns, is overcomplete for the information it actually carries.

blocks.text: 14. A Worked Example
Confirm that (2, 1) and (1, 3) form a valid basis for the 2D plane, then express the point (8, 9) in terms of that basis.

code.content:
B = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 3]]).T
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(B))   # 2, independent, valid basis for 2D space
coords = np.linalg.inv(B).dot(np.array([8, 9]))
print(coords)   # [3. 2.], meaning 3*(2,1) + 2*(1,3) = (8, 9)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Check","Result"],"rows":[["rank equals 2","yes, independent"],["count equals dimension","yes, 2 vectors for 2D space"],["new coordinates","(3, 2)"]]}

blocks.text: Note that this basis (2, 1) and (1, 3) is not orthogonal, their dot product is 2 plus 3 equals 5, not 0, which is why extracting the new coordinates required a full matrix inverse rather than the single dot product shortcut from section 11.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming any set of the right size is automatically a basis, without checking independence, two dependent vectors can never span a space even if the count happens to match the dimension.
Assuming a basis must be orthogonal, most valid bases are not orthogonal at all, orthogonality from section 11 is a desirable convenience, not a requirement.

Confusing the number of vectors in a set with the dimension of the space they live in, a set of 5 vectors in 3D space can span at most a 3 dimensional space, never more, regardless of how many vectors were used.
Forgetting that a change of basis, from section 6, never moves the underlying point, only the numbers used to describe its location relative to a new reference frame.

blocks.text: 16. Practice: Build and Verify a Basis
Take the vectors (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), and (1, 1, 0). Check whether they form a valid basis for 3 dimensional space.

code.content:
C = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 0]])
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(C))   # 2, not 3, so this set cannot span all of 3D space

items: Counting the vectors alone would suggest 3 vectors should be enough for 3D space, matching the trap described in section 13.

Checking rank reveals the truth: all three vectors have a zero in the third position, so none of them can reach anywhere off the xy plane, meaning they only span a 2 dimensional subspace, not the full 3 dimensional space.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

Subspaces, from section 12, follow every one of these same rules at a smaller scale, they have their own dimension, their own valid bases, and that dimension is exactly what rank measures for the row space and column space of a matrix.

A basis is a spanning, independent set of vectors, and dimension is simply how many vectors that basis needs, a fixed number shared by every valid basis of the same space. Coordinates are always relative to a chosen basis, and converting between bases, as covered in section 6, changes those numbers without ever moving the actual point they describe.

This lesson quietly reframes rank, from the rank of matrix lesson, as the dimension of a matrix row or column space, and it sets up the language the singular value decomposition and PCA lessons ahead will use constantly: finding a smaller, more useful basis that still captures what matters most about a dataset.

The singular value decomposition and PCA lessons immediately ahead in this module are best understood as automated, principled ways of finding a smaller, better basis, exactly the dimensionality reduction idea introduced in section 13.
